Overview

Tashkent as a Business Centre

Tashkent is the capital of Uzbekistan and the largest city in Central Asia's most populous country. Its population was about 3.16 million as of October 2025, according to city statistics. The city generated 21.1 percent of national GDP in the first half of 2026, the largest share of any region, with gross regional product of about UZS 226 trillion, up 13.3 percent year on year. Services accounted for almost 68 percent of the city's economy, industry about 20 percent and construction 12 percent. Tashkent concentrates the country's government ministries, banks, the main international airport, foreign-invested businesses and professional advisers, and it is the focus of the government's effort to build an international financial and dispute resolution centre.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Tashkent because most foreign investment into Uzbekistan, including privatisations, public-private partnerships, banking, energy, mining services and real estate development, is negotiated and contracted there. Typical triggers include due diligence on local partners, shareholders and politically exposed persons before a joint venture or acquisition, integrity checks on contractors in state procurement, and support to counsel in disputes before the Tashkent International Arbitration Centre or the economic courts. Uzbekistan's position on trade routes between Russia, China and the rest of Central Asia also prompts counterparty and export control screening for suppliers and distributors dealing through Tashkent intermediaries.

Typical Matters

Investigative Work Connected to Tashkent

01

Partner and shareholder due diligence

Research into Tashkent-based partners, their shareholders and principals before joint ventures, acquisitions and privatisation bids, combining official registration data, court decisions, media in Uzbek and Russian, and corroborated inquiry, with attention to politically exposed persons and family-linked business groups.

02

TIAC and TIFC dispute support

Background research on counterparties, witnesses and experts, and identification of assets relevant to enforcement, for counsel in Tashkent International Arbitration Centre cases and proceedings expected before the Tashkent International Commercial Court, documented so findings can be assessed for evidential use.

03

Procurement and contractor integrity

Checks on contractors, suppliers and consultants bidding for state and municipal contracts or public-private partnerships in Tashkent, covering ownership, related parties, prior performance disputes and adverse media, to support compliance reviews by lenders, investors and international bidders.

04

Trade and diversion screening

Screening of Tashkent distributors, logistics firms and trading companies for links to restricted parties or unusual re-export patterns, supporting export control and sanctions compliance programmes of suppliers whose goods move through Uzbekistan toward neighbouring markets.

05

Real estate and development checks

Ownership and reputational research on developers, contractors and investors in Tashkent's large-scale construction and redevelopment projects, including related companies and financing parties, to support lenders, buyers and partners assessing project risk and counterparties. Sources include court decisions and media.

Local Context

Courts, Records and Institutions in Tashkent

Tashkent International Arbitration Centre

TIAC was created by presidential resolution in November 2018 and has operated under the Chamber of Commerce and Industry since April 2019. Its 2021 rules provide for document production, emergency arbitrators within three business days and an expedited procedure for disputes under USD 3 million, and it agreed a cross-institutional rulebook with the Hong Kong International Arbitration Centre in 2022. It reported 43 international cases in the twelve months to January 2025. International arbitration is governed by the 2021 International Commercial Arbitration Law, based on the UNCITRAL Model Law.

Tashkent International Financial Centre

A constitutional law adopted on 13 July 2026 established the Tashkent International Financial Centre as a special jurisdiction applying the common law of England and Wales where consistent with its own law, with a Financial Services Authority and the Tashkent International Commercial Court. The court sits in two instances in English, with judges of any nationality, and can supervise TIAC arbitrations where parties agree. As of 2026 implementing regulations were still being adopted and the court was not yet operational.

Economic and city courts

Commercial disputes between businesses are heard by the economic courts under the Economic Procedure Code, which since 2022 includes rules on court assistance to arbitration and setting aside awards. The Tashkent City Court has acted in arbitration matters, for example appointing a sole arbitrator in December 2025. Investment disputes involving major investors of at least USD 20 million and state bodies go to a specialised Supreme Court panel; others may be brought in the courts of Tashkent city.

State institutions and registries

Ministries, the Central Bank, state enterprises and the agencies that operate business registration and public procurement are headquartered in Tashkent, and decisions affecting large investments are typically taken there. Company registration data is available through official online services, but ownership above the registered founder level and property records generally require further lawful research and, for certified documents, requests through Uzbek counsel. Proceedings and records are mainly in Uzbek and Russian.

Engagement Standard

How TDSC Scopes Matters in Tashkent

For matters touching Tashkent, TDSC first identifies the decision and the forum: an investment or privatisation, a procurement bid, a TIAC arbitration, a case in the economic courts or, once operational, the Tashkent International Commercial Court. That determines language, evidential standards and which records counsel can obtain. Research combines official registration data, published court decisions and Uzbek- and Russian-language media and open sources, reviewed by native readers. Certified records and any field inquiries are handled through Uzbek counsel and qualified local professionals acting lawfully, with personal data handled under Uzbekistan's personal data law. Trade-related matters are screened for sanctions and export control exposure. TDSC has no office in Tashkent.

TDSC has no office in Tashkent. Engagements are directed from Nashville, Tennessee; where work on the ground is needed, it is performed by appropriately licensed local professionals under a written scope.

Questions

Tashkent: Frequently Asked Questions

Can TDSC support a TIAC arbitration?

Yes, as a consultant to counsel. TDSC can research the opposing party, its shareholders and related companies, profile witnesses and experts, and identify assets relevant to enforcement. Findings are documented with sources so counsel can decide how to use them under the TIAC rules and the 2021 International Commercial Arbitration Law.

What is the Tashkent International Financial Centre?

It is a special jurisdiction in Tashkent created by a constitutional law of July 2026, applying English common law where consistent with its own law, with its own regulator and an English-language international commercial court. Implementing rules were still being adopted in 2026, so parties should confirm its current status with counsel.

Can TDSC identify the real owners of a Tashkent company?

TDSC starts with official registration data on founders and directors, then tests it against court decisions, procurement records, media and corroborated inquiry. We have not identified a public beneficial ownership register in Uzbekistan, so conclusions about ultimate control are stated with their evidential basis and any gaps are made explicit.

Does TDSC screen Tashkent counterparties for sanctions risk?

Yes. TDSC screens Tashkent distributors, logistics firms and trading companies against applicable sanctions lists and researches ownership and trading patterns that may indicate links to restricted parties or onward diversion. Findings support the client's compliance decisions; TDSC does not give legal advice on export control or sanctions law.

Does TDSC have an office or staff in Tashkent?

No. TDSC has no office, staff or address in Tashkent or elsewhere in Uzbekistan. Engagements are managed from Nashville. Where local work is needed, TDSC coordinates qualified and appropriately authorised local professionals and works with the client's Uzbek counsel under a written scope covering legality and data handling.
